# Abstract

Seagrass restoration increasingly relies on seed-based approaches, yet optimal
seeding densities and deployment methods remain poorly resolved. We evaluated
the relative effects of seed density and clam-mediated seed placement on
eelgrass (*Zostera marina*) establishment in a field restoration experiment in
Back Sound, North Carolina. Eelgrass seeds were attached to juvenile live clams
using a gelatin adhesive at densities ranging from 10 to 100 seeds per clam, and
deployed in a fully factorial design crossing seed density with two clam
placement treatments - manually buried or placed on the sediment surface. Plots
were monitored biweekly for shoot establishment and growth over six months.
Shoot density increased through time and was higher in plots receiving greater
numbers of seeds. However, the proportion of seeds that produced shoots did not
vary with seed density, indicating that higher seeding rates yielded more shoots
but did not increase per-seed establishment success. We found no evidence that
initial clam placement (i.e., on the surface or buried in the sediment)
influenced seedling establishment. Similarly, shoot growth trajectories were
broadly comparable between clam placement treatments, though higher seed
densities yielded taller shoots. Although manually buried clams were more
frequently detected during early monitoring and shell fragments were more common
in surface treatments, these differences did not influence restoration outcomes,
suggesting that successful seed deployment occurred despite substantial early
clam loss, potentially because seeds detached from clams soon after deployment.
Our results suggest that increasing seed inputs can increase restoration
outcomes by producing more established shoots, but does not improve the
probability that individual seeds establish. These findings indicate that seed
density per deployment unit can be selected based on desired restoration
configuration and design. Furthermore, manually burying clams provided little
measurable benefit over surface placement, suggesting that less labor-intensive
surface deployment of clams with attached seeds may be sufficient for
large-scale restoration efforts.\newpage

# Introduction

<!--# Mason: 1) Maybe add a few sentences in the beginning about more generalized coastal restoration and the issues with large scale restoration, before jumping into seagrass as the system? 2) And maybe some larger theory on competition and/or density dependence. 3) Perhaps add something in this paragraph about the amount of seeds available for restoration potentially being a bottleneck resource. So if more dense seed additions do have a negative or null effect, then seeds can be more properly allocated to make the most of the stock at hand.  -->

Seagrass meadows provide important ecosystem services, including habitat for
marine organisms, shoreline stabilization, and carbon storage [@barbier2011;
@fourqurean2012], but they continue to decline in many regions worldwide
[@waycott2009; @dunic2021; @peng2026]. As a result, restoration has become an
increasingly important tool for recovering lost seagrass habitat
[@vankatwijk2016]. Seed-based seagrass restoration is especially attractive
because it can be scaled to larger areas than traditional transplant-based
approaches while minimizing damage to donor meadows [@reynolds2012; @orth2000],
but establishment rates are often low and highly variable [@bayraktarov2016;
@orth2020].

One of the challenges in seed-based restoration is determining how many seeds
should be deployed [@orth2003; @gräfnings2023]. Increasing seed density may
increase the total number of seedlings that establish simply because more seeds
are available. However, changing planting density may also alter interactions
among individual seeds or seedlings. At higher densities, these interactions
could reduce establishment through competition for space or light, or enhance it
through intraspecific facilitation [@zhang2021; @gräfnings2023]. From a
restoration perspective, it is important to know whether adding more seeds
increases the number of established shoots, improves the probability that
individual seeds establish, or both. It is also unclear whether increasing seed
density results in proportional increases in shoot establishment or whether
density-dependent processes alter establishment success.

Recent restoration studies have increasingly suggested incorporating positive
interactions among species to enhance success [@valdez2020; @zhang2021]. In
seagrass systems, associated organisms can facilitate seagrass through diverse
mechanisms, including reducing herbivory [@morton2026], enhancing nutrient
availability [@peterson2001], and improving water clarity [@wall2008]. Bivalves
in particular have received considerable attention because they can enhance
seagrass biomass, growth, patch expansion, and resilience to disturbance through
several of these pathways [@peterson2001; @wall2008; @donaher2021; @zhang2021].
While incorporating facilitating species such as bivalves represents a promising
restoration approach, questions remain about how these interactions can best be
incorporated.

Building on these positive interactions, attaching seagrass seeds to live clams
may provide a novel means of harnessing their natural burrowing behavior for
seed delivery. As clams burrow, they may carry attached seeds below the sediment
surface where conditions are favorable for germination. This approach extends
the use of positive species interactions in restoration by creating a functional
link between species that harnesses natural behavior for a new restoration
function [@silliman2026]. However, it remains unclear whether clams burrow
rapidly enough after deployment to protect both themselves and attached seeds
from predation or physical disturbance. Manually burying seeded clams may reduce
this initial vulnerability but also increases deployment effort and may limit
scalability. Whether natural clam burrowing is sufficient for seed deployment
will affect the scalability of clam-mediated seagrass restoration.

In this study, we attached eelgrass (*Zostera marina*) seeds to live hard clams
(*Mercenaria mercenaria)*, and tested how seed density and clam placement
influence eelgrass establishment in a field restoration experiment in North
Carolina. Specifically, we asked whether increasing seed density increases
establishment, whether manually burying clams improves establishment relative to
placing them on the sediment surface, and whether these effects interact. We
quantified total shoot establishment, per-seed establishment, and shoot height
through time to evaluate how restoration efficiency changes across a range of
seeding densities.

# Methods

## *Seed retrieval and storage*

Reproductive *Zostera marina* shoots were collected from seagrass beds in Back
Sound, NC in May 2025. Shoots were held in flow-through seawater tanks indoors
until mature seeds were naturally released. Released seeds were collected from
the bottom of the tank and stored in mesh bags in a flow-through tank. While
this storage tank was exposed to general ambient light conditions, the mesh bags
reduced overall light exposure. Before deployment, 100 seeds were randomly
selected to test for viability using tetrazolium staining [@jarvis2014], with
89% of seeds classified as viable.

## *Planting experiment*

To test how seed planting density and clam placement influences seagrass
establishment and growth, we conducted a field experiment near Harker’s Island,
North Carolina. Juvenile live clams (*Mercenaria mercenaria;* \~2 cm shell
length) were sourced from aquaculture facilities at Carteret Community College
and stored in flow-through seawater tanks prior to deployment. Seagrass seeds
were attached to live clams using a gelatin-based bioglue at one of ten density
levels, spanning 10-100 seeds per clam in increments of 10 seeds. Seed planting
density was crossed with two clam placement treatments (manually buried or
placed on sediment surface) in a fully factorial design with four replicates per
treatment combination (80 plots total).

The bioglue was prepared by dissolving dry gelatin powder in saltwater (35 ppt)
to a final concentration of 9% (w/v). The solution was heated to 35°C until
fully dissolved and then cooled to 25°C before application, as exposure to high
temperatures can reduce viability [@pan2011]. A thin layer of bioglue was
pipetted onto one shell from each clam and allowed to partially set before seeds
were arranged in a single layer and covered with a second thin coat of glue.
Clams with seeds were refrigerated at 9°C for 30 minutes to allow the glue to
solidify, then transported to the field in coolers and deployed the same day.
The total time from initial glue preparation through field deployment was less
than four hours, during which all seeds remained attached to clams; preliminary
lab trials indicated that adhesive dissolved and seeds detached from clams
within 8-12 hours.

Clams were either manually buried to a depth of 2 cm [@jørgensen2019] or placed
on the sediment surface to allow natural self-burial. Each clam was positioned
at the center of a 0.25 m x 0.25 m plot, with the corner of each plot marked
with a lawn staple to facilitate resampling. Plots were arranged in a grid with
0.5 m spacing in a sandy area located at least 10 m away from adjacent salt
marsh, oyster reef, and seagrass habitat.

Plots were monitored approximately every two weeks from November 2025 through
April 2026. During each survey, we recorded the number of live shoots and
measured the height of up to five randomly selected shoots to the nearest
millimeter. During the first four sampling dates, we assessed clam presence by
searching for siphon holes and gently probing the sediment surface to detect the
edge of the clam shell. We avoided excavating clams to limit seedling
disturbance. For each plot, we recorded whether a live clam was confirmed,
whether shell fragments or empty shells were present (as evidence of potential
clam predation/mortality), or whether no clam evidence was detected.

```{r setup}
# Setup -------------------------------------------------------------------------
library(readxl)
library(tidyverse)
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(glmmTMB)
library(DHARMa)
library(gt)
library(ggeffects)
library(emmeans) 
library(patchwork)
library(broom.mixed)

# Helper function that will add significance to p values:
add_significance <- function(df) {df %>%
    mutate(significance = factor(case_when(p_value < 0.001 ~ "***",
                                           p_value < 0.01 ~ "**",
                                           p_value < 0.05 ~ "*",
                                           is.na(p_value) ~ "NA",
                                           TRUE ~ "NS"), 
                                 levels = c("***", "**", "*", "NS", "NA")))
}

# Helper function that will clean up the fixed effects:
clean_fixed_effects <- function(df){df %>% 
    as.data.frame() %>% 
    rownames_to_column("term") %>% 
    rename(p = `Pr(>Chisq)`) %>% 
    rename_with(~"chisq", matches("LR Chisq|Chisq")) %>%
    janitor::clean_names() %>% 
    mutate(chisq = round(chisq, 2),
           p = round(p, 3))
}

# Read data from Excel file 
dat_raw <- read_xlsx("data/seed-density.xlsx", na = "NA") 

# Build ------------------------------------------------------------------------
# - density is continuous
# - burial is a factor
# - plot_id identifies the repeated-measures unit
# - time is measured as days since the first sampling date
# - shoot_count is the number of shoots observed at each sampling event

dat <- dat_raw %>% 
  mutate(plot_id = factor(plot_id),
         burial = factor(burial_treatment,
                         levels = c(0, 1),
                         labels = c("Buried", "Surface")),
         date = lubridate::ymd(date),
         time_days = as.numeric(date - date('2025-10-31')),
         length_cm_5 = as.numeric(length_cm_5)) %>% 
  # monitoring on 4 Jan 2026 was incomplete because poor conditions (remove)
  filter(date != '2026-01-04') %>% 
  # bin densities in case useful for later plotting
  mutate(density_group = case_when(seed_density <= 30 ~ "Low\n10–30 seeds",
                                   seed_density <= 70 ~ "Medium\n40–70 seeds",
                                   seed_density >= 80 ~ "High\n80–100 seeds"),
         density_group = factor(density_group,
                                levels = c("Low\n10–30 seeds", "Medium\n40–70 seeds",
                                           "High\n80–100 seeds"))) %>% 
  # calculate proportion established relative to seed density
   mutate(est_prob = shoot_count/seed_density) %>% 
   mutate(failures = seed_density - shoot_count)

  
```

## *Data analyses*

To evaluate how seed planting density and clam placement influenced restoration
outcomes, we quantified three complementary response variables: shoot density,
per-seed establishment, and shoot growth. Shoot density was quantified as the
number of shoots per plot (0.0625 m^2^). Per-seed establishment was quantified
as the number of observed live shoots relative to the number of seeds initially
planted in each plot. Both shoot density and per-seed establishment were
analyzed for the final sampling date: `r format(max(dat$date), "%B %d, %Y")`.
Shoot growth was quantified as mean shoot height through time.

Final shoot density was analyzed using a generalized linear model with a
negative binomial distribution and log link. Per-seed establishment was analyzed
using a beta-binomial distribution with a logit link. Both models included seed
planting density (continuous), clam placement (factor; buried or surface), and
their interaction as fixed effects. Mean shoot height was analyzed using a
linear mixed-effects model with plot included as a random intercept to account
for repeated measurements through time. Fixed effects included seed planting
density, clam placement treatment, sampling date, and the interaction between
seed planting density and sampling date.

To evaluate whether clam placement treatment influenced early detection of
deployed clams, we fit a binomial generalized linear model with clam placement
treatment as the predictor and the presence or absence of a live clam during the
first two post-deployment surveys as the response variable. A clam was
classified as present if it was observed during either survey. Although
occurrence of shells or shell fragments on the sediment surface were also
recorded, these observations were not used as the primary response because shell
observations were occasionally followed by subsequent live clam observations
within the same plot, making shell evidence an ambiguous indicator of deployed
clam fate. Only the first two surveys were included because they occurred before
the first seedlings were observed. We then fit exploratory models for final
shoot density, per-seed establishment, and final shoot height that included seed
planting density, clam placement treatment, their interaction, and the binary
clam indicator as an additional fixed effect to evaluate whether early clam
presence explained variation in restoration outcomes after accounting for the
experimental treatments.

Significance of fixed effects was evaluated using Type II ANOVA ($\chi^2$
tests), and model assumptions were assessed using simulated residual diagnostics
(DHARMa; @hartig2026) to evaluate dispersion and zero inflation. Model
predictions and estimated marginal means were used to visualize treatment
effects and quantify effect sizes. All analyses were conducted in R version
4.5.3 [@rcoreteam2025] & RStudio (version 2025.09.2+418; @positteam2025).

```{r build-dataframes}
#| include: false

# Calculate treatment-level means through time
dat_means <- dat %>% 
  group_by(date, seed_density, burial) %>% 
  summarize(shoot_count_mean = mean(shoot_count),
            shoot_count_sd = sd(shoot_count),
            shoot_count_n = n()) %>% 
  mutate(shoot_count_se = shoot_count_sd/sqrt(shoot_count_n))

# Create predation dataframe from clam checks
pred <- dat %>% 
  select(date:clam_code, burial) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(clam_code)) %>%
  filter(date < "2026-04-01") %>% 
  mutate(date = as.factor(date),
         clam_code_label = case_when(clam_code == "D" ~ "Empty shell",
                                     clam_code == "L" ~ "Live",
                                     clam_code == "S" ~ "Shell fragments",
                                     clam_code == "N" ~ "Nothing"))

# Create growth dataframe
dat_growth <- dat %>% 
  select(date, plot_id, seed_density, burial, time_days, 
         shoot_count, starts_with("length")) %>% 
  pivot_longer(starts_with("length"), 
               names_to = "length_replicate", values_to = "length_cm") %>%
  filter(!is.na(length_cm)) %>% 
  group_by(date, plot_id, seed_density, burial, time_days) %>% 
  summarize(length_cm_mean = mean(length_cm) ,
            length_cm_sd   = sd(length_cm),
            length_cm_n    = n(), .groups = 'drop') %>% 
  mutate(length_cm_se = length_cm_sd/sqrt(length_cm_n)) %>% 
  mutate(time_factor = factor(time_days,
                              levels = c('47', '78','91','106','152','168'),
                              labels = c("Dec 17", "Jan 17", "Jan 30", "Feb 14", "Apr 1", "Apr 17")))

# Build "shoot establishment" models using last sampling date (April)
dat_end <- dat %>% 
  filter(date == max(date))

# Summarize to show treatment means and error
dat_end_summary <- dat_end %>% 
  group_by(seed_density, burial) %>% 
  summarize(mean_count = mean(shoot_count),
            se_count = sd(shoot_count) / sqrt(n()),
            .groups = "drop")

# Clam observations from first two surveys
dat_clam <- dat %>%
  filter(date %in% c("2025-11-05","2025-11-17")) %>%
  mutate(live_clam = if_else(clam_code == "L", 1, 0),
         shell_frag = if_else(clam_code == "S", 1, 0),
         empty_shell = if_else(clam_code == "D", 1, 0)) %>% 
  group_by(plot_id) %>%
  summarize(ever_live  = any(live_clam == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
            ever_shell = any(shell_frag == 1 | empty_shell == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(dat_end, by = "plot_id") %>% 
  rowwise() %>% 
  mutate(length_cm_mean = mean(c_across(length_cm_1:length_cm_5), na.rm = TRUE))
 
```

```{r m_count}
#| include: false

# Test whether more seeds = more shoots  
m_count <- glmmTMB(shoot_count ~ seed_density * burial, family = nbinom2, data = dat_end)

summary(m_count)

# Check diagnostics
res_count <- simulateResiduals(m_count)
plot(res_count)
testDispersion(res_count)
testZeroInflation(res_count)

# Check the fixed effects and save outputs for results text
m_count_tests <-  car::Anova(m_count, type = 2) %>% clean_fixed_effects()
  
# Get the values for the results text
# From the m_count model:
density_chisq <- filter(m_count_tests, term == "seed_density") %>% pull(chisq)
density_p     <- filter(m_count_tests, term == "seed_density") %>% pull(p)
burial_chisq  <- filter(m_count_tests, term == "burial")  %>% pull(chisq)
burial_p      <- filter(m_count_tests, term == "burial")  %>% pull(p) 
int_chisq     <- filter(m_count_tests, term == "seed_density:burial") %>% pull(chisq)
int_p         <- filter(m_count_tests, term == "seed_density:burial") %>% pull(p)

# Get the expected shoots counts for 10 vs 100 seeds, averaged over burial treatment
m_count_pred <- emmeans(m_count, ~ seed_density, 
                        at = list(seed_density = c(10, 100)),
                        type = "response") %>%  
  summary() %>% 
  janitor::clean_names() %>% 
  mutate(across(c(response, se, asymp_lcl, asymp_ucl), ~round(.x, 3)))

shoot10      <- filter(m_count_pred, seed_density == 10) %>% pull(response) %>% round(., 1)
shoot10_low  <- filter(m_count_pred, seed_density == 10) %>% pull(asymp_lcl) %>% round(., 1)
shoot10_high <- filter(m_count_pred, seed_density == 10) %>% pull(asymp_ucl) %>% round(., 1)

shoot100      <- filter(m_count_pred, seed_density == 100) %>% pull(response) %>% round(., 1)
shoot100_low  <- filter(m_count_pred, seed_density == 100) %>% pull(asymp_lcl) %>% round(., 1)
shoot100_high <- filter(m_count_pred, seed_density == 100) %>% pull(asymp_ucl) %>% round(., 1)

# Estimate the average density effect
m_count_trend <- emtrends(m_count, ~1, var = "seed_density") |>
  summary()

# Convert avg density effect te expected % increase in final shoot count per 10 additional seeds
pct10      <- round((exp(m_count_trend$seed_density.trend * 10) - 1) * 100, 1)
pct10_low  <- round((exp(m_count_trend$asymp.LCL * 10) - 1) * 100, 1)
pct10_high <- round((exp(m_count_trend$asymp.UCL * 10) - 1) * 100, 1)

# Generate predictions for the figure
m_count_pred_all <- ggpredict(m_count, terms = c("seed_density[10:100]", "burial")) %>% 
  rename(seed_density = x, burial = group)

```

```{r m_prop}
#| include: false

# Start with a binomial mixed model where the response is the number of shoots relative to the initial seeds. Each plot started with a set number of seeds, and each sampling event we see a number of shoots. As a binomial process, the "successes" are the seeds that produce shoots and the "failures" are seeds that didn't. Answers the question "out of # seeds, how many became shoots?" It also accounts for the different starting number of seeds (different number of 'chances') and explicitly models the probability of establishment per seed, answering questions about density-dependent net shoot establishment.

# Test if higher density changes establishment efficiency
m_prop <- glmmTMB(cbind(shoot_count, seed_density - shoot_count) ~ seed_density * burial,
                  family = betabinomial(), data = dat_end)

summary(m_prop)

# Check diagnostics
res_prop <- simulateResiduals(m_prop)
plot(res_prop)
testDispersion(res_prop)
testZeroInflation(res_prop)

# Check the fixed effects
m_prop_tests <- car::Anova(m_prop, type = 2) %>% clean_fixed_effects()

# Get the values for the results text
# From the m_prop model:
m_prop_density_chisq <- filter(m_prop_tests, term == "seed_density") %>% pull(chisq)
m_prop_density_p     <- filter(m_prop_tests, term == "seed_density") %>% pull(p)
m_prop_burial_chisq  <- filter(m_prop_tests, term == "burial")  %>% pull(chisq)
m_prop_burial_p      <- filter(m_prop_tests, term == "burial")  %>% pull(p) 
m_prop_int_chisq     <- filter(m_prop_tests, term == "seed_density:burial") %>% pull(chisq)
m_prop_int_p         <- filter(m_prop_tests, term == "seed_density:burial") %>% pull(p) 

# Generate predictions for the figure
m_prop_pred_all <- ggpredict(m_prop, terms = c("seed_density[10:100]", "burial")) %>% 
  rename(seed_density = x, burial = group)

```

```{r m_growth}
#| include: false
 
# Build model that examines shoot height through time
m_growth <- lmer(length_cm_mean ~ seed_density * time_factor + burial + (1 | plot_id),
               data = dat_growth)

m_growth2 <- lmer(length_cm_mean ~ seed_density * time_days * burial + (1 | plot_id),
               data = dat_growth)

m_growth3 <- lmer(length_cm_mean ~ seed_density * time_factor * burial + (1 | plot_id),
               data = dat_growth)

m_growth4 <- lmer(length_cm_mean ~ seed_density * time_days + burial + (1 | plot_id),
               data = dat_growth)

anova(m_growth, m_growth2, m_growth3, m_growth4) 

# Most supported model has time as a factor and only 2-way interaction density * time

summary(m_growth)

# Check out the diagnostics 
growth_res <- simulateResiduals(m_growth)
plot(growth_res) # wow looks surprisingly good

# Quick check to see what this looks like
plot(effects::allEffects(m_growth), multiline = T, confint = list(style = 'auto'))
# seems like differences in densities emerged in Feb and continued from there

# Check fixed effects with the anova:
m_growth_tests <- car::Anova(m_growth, type = 2) %>% clean_fixed_effects()

# Get the values for the results text
# From the m_growth model:
m_growth_density_chisq <- filter(m_growth_tests, term == "seed_density") %>% pull(chisq)
m_growth_density_p     <- filter(m_growth_tests, term == "seed_density") %>% pull(p)
m_growth_time_chisq    <- filter(m_growth_tests, term == "time_factor")  %>% pull(chisq)
m_growth_time_p        <- filter(m_growth_tests, term == "time_factor")  %>% pull(p) 
m_growth_burial_chisq  <- filter(m_growth_tests, term == "burial")  %>% pull(chisq)
m_growth_burial_p      <- filter(m_growth_tests, term == "burial")  %>% pull(p) 
m_growth_int_chisq     <- filter(m_growth_tests, term == "seed_density:time_factor") %>% 
  pull(chisq)
m_growth_int_p         <- filter(m_growth_tests, term == "seed_density:time_factor") %>% 
  pull(p) 


# Shoot height increased through time, and the effect of planting density 
# varied among sampling dates (density × sampling date interaction, Table X).

# Use emtrends to identify when the differences in heights across densities emerged
emtrends(m_growth, ~ time_factor, var = "seed_density")


emm <- emmeans(m_growth, ~ seed_density | time_factor,
               at = list(seed_density = c(10, 100)))

pairs(emm)

# Generate predictions for the figure
growth_pred <- ggpredict(m_growth, 
                         terms = c("time_factor", "seed_density [10,20,40,60,80,100]"))

```

```{r m_predation}
#| include: false

# Burial effects on clam fate
m_live_fate  <- glm(ever_live ~ burial, family = binomial, data = dat_clam)

plot(simulateResiduals(m_live_fate)) # good

m_shell_fate <- glm(ever_shell ~ burial, family = binomial, data = dat_clam)

# Clam fate effects on final shoot establishment
m_live_shoots  <- glmmTMB(shoot_count ~ seed_density * burial + ever_live,
                          family = nbinom2, data = dat_clam)

plot(simulateResiduals(m_live_shoots)) 

# Clam fate effects on per-seed establishment
m_live_prop <- glmmTMB(cbind(shoot_count, 
                             seed_density - shoot_count) ~ seed_density * burial + ever_live,
                       family = betabinomial(), data = dat_clam)

plot(simulateResiduals(m_live_prop)) 

# Clam fate effects on final shoot height
m_live_height <- glm(length_cm_mean ~ seed_density * burial + ever_live, data = dat_clam)

plot(simulateResiduals(m_live_height))
summary(m_live_height)

# Check fixed effects
m_live_fate_tests   <- car::Anova(m_live_fate, type = 2) %>% clean_fixed_effects()
m_live_shoot_tests  <- car::Anova(m_live_shoots, type = 2) %>% clean_fixed_effects()
m_live_prop_tests   <- car::Anova(m_live_prop, type = 2) %>% clean_fixed_effects()
m_live_height_tests <- car::Anova(m_live_height, type = 2) %>% clean_fixed_effects()

# Pull values for results text
m_live_fate_chisq   <- filter(m_live_fate_tests, term == "burial") %>% pull(chisq)
m_live_fate_p       <- filter(m_live_fate_tests, term == "burial") %>% pull(p)
m_live_shoot_chisq  <- filter(m_live_shoot_tests, term == "ever_live") %>% pull(chisq)
m_live_shoot_p      <- filter(m_live_shoot_tests, term == "ever_live") %>% pull(p)
m_live_prop_chisq   <- filter(m_live_prop_tests, term == "ever_live") %>% pull(chisq)
m_live_prop_p       <- filter(m_live_prop_tests, term == "ever_live") %>% pull(p)
m_live_height_chisq <- filter(m_live_height_tests, term == "ever_live") %>% pull(chisq)
m_live_height_p     <- filter(m_live_height_tests, term == "ever_live") %>% pull(p)

# How many plots had shells:
n_shell_surface <- sum(dat_clam$ever_shell[dat_clam$burial == "Surface"])
n_shell_buried <- sum(dat_clam$ever_shell[dat_clam$burial == "Buried"])

```

# Results

Shoot establishment increased significantly with seed planting density ($\chi^2$
= `r density_chisq`, *p* = `r density_p`), whereas both clam placement ($\chi^2$
= `r burial_chisq`, *p* = `r burial_p`) and the interaction between seed
planting density and clam placement ($\chi^2$ = `r int_chisq`, *p* = `r int_p`)
were not significant (@fig-1). Each additional 10 seeds planted increased the
expected number of established shoots by `r pct10`% (95% CI:
`r pct10_low`-`r pct10_high`%). Model predictions indicated that increasing
planting density from 10 to 100 seeds increased the expected number of
established shoots from `r shoot10` (95% CI: `r shoot10_low`-`r shoot10_high`)
to `r shoot100` (95% CI: `r shoot100_low`-`r shoot100_high`).

Shoot establishment increased throughout the experiment across all treatments
(@fig-2). Following the onset of shoot establishment in December, higher
planting densities accumulated shoots more rapidly than lower planting
densities, resulting in progressively greater differences in shoot establishment
through time.

This increase reflected greater shoot establishment rather than higher per-seed
establishment: while shoot density increased with seed density, the *proportion*
of seeds that produced shoots did not. Per-seed establishment was not
significantly affected by seed density ($\chi^2$ = `r m_prop_density_chisq`*, p*
= `r m_prop_density_p`), clam placement ($\chi^2$ = `r m_prop_burial_chisq`, *p*
= `r m_prop_burial_p`), or their interaction ($\chi^2$ = `r m_prop_int_chisq` ,
*p* = `r m_prop_int_p`) (@fig-1). Model-predicted per-seed establishment ranged
from approximately 5% to 12% across planting densities, although these
differences were not statistically significant.

Mean shoot height increased throughout the experiment ($\chi^2$ =
`r m_growth_time_chisq` , *p*
`r if_else(m_growth_time_p < 0.001, "< 0.001", paste("= ", m_growth_time_p))`),
and the relationship between seed planting density and shoot height varied
across sampling dates (seed density x sampling date: $\chi^2$ =
`r m_growth_int_chisq` , *p* = `r m_growth_int_p`). Clam placement did not
affect shoot height ($\chi^2$ = `r m_growth_burial_chisq` , *p* =
`r m_growth_burial_p`). Model predictions indicated that shoot height was
similar among planting densities during the first three months, whereas shoots
in higher-density treatments were consistently taller during the latter half of
the experiment (@fig-3).

Clam placement influenced the short-term fate of deployed clams (@fig-4).
Manually buried clams were more likely to be found during the first two
post-deployment surveys than surface-deployed clams ($\chi^2$ =
`r m_live_fate_chisq`, *p* = `r m_live_fate_p`). Shell fragments were also
observed more frequently in surface treatments (n = `r n_shell_surface`,
`r n_shell_surface/40*100`%) compared to manually buried treatments (n =
`r n_shell_buried`, `r n_shell_buried/40*100`%). However, confirmed clam
presence was not associated with either final shoot establishment ($\chi^2$ =
`r m_live_shoot_chisq`, *p* = `r m_live_shoot_p`), per-seed establishment
($\chi^2$ = `r m_live_prop_chisq`, *p* = `r m_live_prop_p`), or final shoot
height ($\chi^2$ = `r m_live_height_chisq`, *p* = `r m_live_height_p`) after
accounting for seed planting density and clam placement. Seed planting density
remained the only significant predictor in the model of final shoot
establishment, and was marginally significant for both per-seed establishment
and final shoot height (Table S1).

# Discussion

Our study suggests that attaching eelgrass seeds to live clams offers a viable
seed deployment strategy for restoration. Increasing seed planting density
produced proportionally more established shoots while maintaining similar
per-seed establishment. Likewise, manually burying clams increased short-term
clam retention but did not improve shoot establishment or growth compared to
surface deployment. These findings indicate that clam-mediated seed deployment
can provide predictable restoration outcomes across a wide range of planting
densities, offering practitioners flexibility in how limited seed resources are
allocated during restoration efforts.

The positive relationship between planting density and shoot establishment is
consistent with previous seed-based eelgrass restoration studies, where planting
more seeds generally results in more established seedlings or shoots [@orth2003;
@marion2010; @orth2012]. However, relatively few studies have examined
establishment efficiency on a per-seed basis. Although @gräfnings2023 reported
lower per-seed recruitment at a higher seed density using seed injection in the
Dutch Wadden Sea (2 vs. 20 seeds per injection), per-seed establishment remained
constant across the 10-100 seeds per clam evaluated here. This lack of density
dependence suggests that neither competition nor facilitation strongly
influenced seedling establishment during the first growing season. Instead,
establishment appears to have been governed by seed viability and local
environmental conditions rather than interactions among neighboring seedlings.
Whether positive or negative density dependence emerges at substantially lower
or higher planting densities, or later during seagrass meadow development,
remains an important question for future work.

One of the primary uncertainties surrounding clam-mediated seed deployment was
whether natural burrowing would rapidly incorporate attached seeds into the
sediment. Although manually burying clams increased the probability of
relocating live clams during the first two post-deployment surveys, this
difference did not translate into greater shoot establishment, per-seed
establishment, or shoot growth. Likewise, overall clam persistence was low in
both treatments, and surface-deployed plots contained more shell fragments and
empty shells, suggesting greater predation or mortality following deployment.
Juvenile clams are susceptible to predation by blue crabs, mud crabs,
gastropods, and cownose rays, making predation a plausible explanation for the
observed losses [@micheli1997; @peterson1982]. Collectively, this suggests that
seed incorporation occurred rapidly regardless of clam fate. A likely
explanation is that seeds detached from clams soon after deployment. Preliminary
laboratory trials indicated that the gelatin adhesive retained attached seeds
for approximately 8-12 hours, potentially allowing sufficient time for natural
burrowing before seed release. The duration of seed attachment is therefore
likely to be an important consideration in the design of this restoration
approach, with the objective of timing seed release with initial sediment
incorporation rather than maintaining long-term attachment.

The limited relationship between clam persistence and restoration outcomes
should not be interpreted as evidence that bivalves do not facilitate seagrass
restoration. Previous studies have shown that persistent bivalve populations can
enhance seagrass performance [@peterson2001; @zhang2021; @donaher2021]. More
broadly, positive species interactions are increasingly recognized as important
drivers of restoration success, although their strength often depends on
ecological context and the stage of ecosystem development [@silliman2024]. In
contrast, our experiment evaluated only the first six months post-deployment and
included a single juvenile clam per plot. This density and timescale was likely
insufficient to generate the ecosystem engineering effects typically associated
with mature bivalve populations, and any facilitative effects are also likely to
depend on local environmental conditions, including sediment characteristics and
nutrient availability. Instead, our results highlight that successful seed
deployment and early establishment did not depend on prolonged clam persistence
during the initial establishment phase.

Although planting density did not influence establishment efficiency, shoots in
higher-density treatments became taller later in the experiment. Increased shoot
height at higher planting densities may represent the early development of
positive interactions among neighboring shoots, or increased competition for
light as local canopy density increased. As patches expand, greater local shoot
density could reduce hydrodynamic stress or enhance sediment stabilization,
processes known to reinforce seagrass growth and persistence [@fonseca1986;
@vankatwijk2009]. Since these responses emerged only after shoot establishment,
they likely reflect post-establishment interactions rather than mechanisms
affecting initial seed establishment.

From a restoration perspective, these findings shift the practical question from
how many seeds should be planted to how limited seed resources should be
allocated. Seed availability frequently constrains the scale of seagrass
restoration [@orth2003; @vankatwijk2016], making efficient seed allocation a
central management challenge. Because per-seed establishment remained similar
across planting densities, practitioners can select seed density per clam based
on desired restoration outcomes without sacrificing per-seed performance. For
example, concentrating many seeds on fewer clams is expected to produce dense
patches, whereas distributing the same number of seeds among more clams would
produce a similar number of established shoots distributed across a larger area.
Whether these alternative planting strategies ultimately produce comparable
restoration outcomes over longer timescales remains unknown, as
density-dependent facilitation or competition may emerge as restored patches
develop. Determining the planting and deployment design that best promotes
long-term seagrass expansion will therefore require longer-term studies that
evaluate how planting density influences survival, patch development, and
seagrass persistence under different environmental conditions.

Overall, our results demonstrate that live hard clams can function as effective
seed deployment agents despite limited long-term persistence. Early restoration
success was determined primarily by seed supply rather than clam placement or
persistence, and establishment efficiency remained consistent across a broad
range of planting densities. These findings support clam-mediated seed
deployment as a practical addition to the growing suite of seed-based
restoration approaches, and illustrate how harnessing natural organismal
behaviors can inform the design of restoration techniques that work with, rather
than against, ecological processes [@silliman2026]. Together, these findings
provide a framework for optimizing seed allocation and deployment at broader
scales.

# Figure Captions

**Figure 1.** Clam-mediated seed deployment and subsequent seagrass
establishment. A) Juvenile hard clam (*Mercenaria mercenaria*) with eelgrass
(*Zostera marina*) seeds attached using a gelatin adhesive prior to deployment.
B) Experimental plot showing seagrass within the PVC monitoring quadrat used for
repeated surveys in April 2026, five months post-deployment.

**Figure 2.** Effects of seed planting density on (A) final shoot count and (B)
establishment probability at the final sampling point. Establishment probability
was calculated as the proportion of planted seeds that produced observable
shoots, integrating seed retention, germination, and early seedling survival.
Points represent individual plots. Lines show model predictions (±95% CI) by
clam placement treatment: on the sediment surface (purple triangles, dashed
line) or manually buried (green circles, solid line).

**Figure 3.** Temporal patterns in shoot establishment across seed planting
density groups and clam placement treatments. For visualization, seed planting
densities were grouped into low (10-30 seeds), medium (40-70 seeds), and high
(80-100 seeds) categories. Points represent the average shoot count per plot
(±SE) at each sampling date, averaged across all plots within each seed density
group and clam placement treatment. Green circles and solid lines indicate
manually buried clams; purple triangles and dashed lines indicate clams placed
on the sediment surface.

**Figure 4.** Effects of seed planting density on mean shoot height (cm) over
the course of the experiment. Lines show model-predicted mean shoot height (±95%
CI) from a linear mixed effects model, averaged across clam placement
treatments. Darker blue lines indicate higher seed densities. For clarity, only
six seed densities are shown; ommitted densities follow the same trend.

**Figure 5.** Effects of clam placement treatment on short-term clam fate.
Model-predicted probabilities (±95% CI) of observing (A) a live clam and (B)
shell evidence (shell fragments or empty shells) during the first two
post-deployment surveys from binomial generalized linear models.

dat_density_group_means <- dat %>%
  group_by(date, burial, density_group) %>%
  summarise(shoot_count_mean = mean(shoot_count, na.rm = TRUE),
            shoot_count_se = sd(shoot_count, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
            establishment_mean = mean(shoot_count / seed_density, na.rm = TRUE),
            establishment_se = sd(shoot_count / seed_density, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
            .groups = "drop")

ggplot(dat_density_group_means,
       aes(date, shoot_count_mean, 
           color = burial, fill = burial, group = burial, pch = burial, linetype = burial)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = shoot_count_mean - shoot_count_se,
                    ymax = shoot_count_mean + shoot_count_se),
                alpha = 0.2, color = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~density_group) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#1b9e77", "#7570b3")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1b9e77", "#7570b3")) +
  labs(x = "",
       y = expression("Shoot count per 0.0625 m"^2),
       color = "Clam placement",
       fill = "Clam placement",
       pch = "Clam placement",
       linetype = "Clam placement") +
  theme_classic() +

        legend.position = "top")
